This summer

Bars: hectares burned each day. Line: how dry the forest is (0 to 100 %). Blue: days with rain. Bolt: lightning.

Every fire

Each fire that has burned out is a dot: how much of its part of the forest was green (trees or grass) when it was lit, and how much of that part it burned. Grey when damp, amber when dry; ringed: lightning. Small grey points: storm strikes. Roads and gaps split the forest into parts.

Fire sizes

All fires so far, yours, lightning's and the storm's: how often each size occurs. Both axes are logarithmic, so tiny and huge fires fit on one chart. Crews make fires smaller, so they shift both charts; the storm plays without them.

About this toy

A toy, not a model. The map is real: the Eilenriede, Hannover's city forest, as OpenStreetMap outlines it, with all the parts it counts in (among them the Tiergarten, Hermann-Löns-Park and the Seelhorst), its paths, roads, streams and clearings, cut into cells of 25 by 25 metres. The rules are made up for play: a burning cell lights its neighbours with a chance set by dryness and wind; paths and tracks catch less often; roads, water and buildings do not burn; with wind an ember now and then jumps a few cells ahead. Leaf types come from OpenStreetMap where it has them; in the toy mixed wood catches a little more readily than broadleaved wood, a rule of the toy, not a fact. Each day the forest dries a little more, burnt and cut ground slowly grows back, and clouds drift over: tap one for rain. When it is dry, clouds can throw lightning. Paths, tracks and clearings count as ground that can burn.

The city around the forest, about two kilometres of it on every side, with its buildings, main streets, railways, water, a few landmarks and the names of the districts, also comes from OpenStreetMap and is there to show where you are. In the toy it never burns: fire stops at the forest edge, and embers that land in the city go out. The city is drawn flat, like a map at night, so the forest stands out. The names on the map are the ones OpenStreetMap gives.

How to play: tap to light a fire, hold for a bigger one, swipe across the map to set the wind (direction and length of the swipe). With Cut, drag to clear a firebreak; with Plant, drag to plant trees. Pinch or scroll to zoom. Storm strikes a copy of the forest 300 times.

Fire crews: the red lights are real fire stations from OpenStreetMap, with the names it gives (some shortened). In the toy a crew leaves on its own once a fire has burned a while, or when you tap its station. It drives mostly along streets and forest roads (and across open ground or through the trees where it must), puts out the burning cells within reach and wets the trees around it so they do not catch for a while, until its water runs out; then it drives back to fill up. How fast the crews drive, how far they reach, how much they put out and how long the wet trees hold are made-up rules. They say nothing about the real fire brigade, its stations or how quickly it arrives.

Nothing here describes the real forest or its fire risk, and every number on this page describes the toy only.

Spreading through a random grid like this is studied in mathematics as percolation (Broadbent and Hammersley, 1957, doi:10.1017/S0305004100032680).
